# Label-Free Parkinson's Disease Screening from Face and Voice through Mechanistic Interpretability

- **Authors**: Jiaheng Su, Yu Sun
- **Venue**: cs.LG
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08976>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08976v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.50

## In one line

Builds a Parkinson's screen from control data alone using a contrastive activation direction derived from synthetically degraded healthy speech and a nearest-neighbour anomaly score in face-encoder space, and gives a measurable precondition -- positive cosine between the synthetic and real disease directions -- that predicts in advance which modality the steering primitive will work on.

## Problem

Supervised video screens for Parkinson's disease need labelled corpora that require clinical recruitment and expert annotation, so they are small, class-imbalanced, subject-confounded and prone to learning shortcuts. Healthy talking-head video is effectively unlimited while labelled disease video is scarce, which suggests treating the disease as a deviation from healthy in a learned representation. The open question is whether an interpretability primitive built from a proxy contrast -- degrading healthy examples toward what the disease looks like -- yields a direction that actually points at the real disease, and whether that can be checked rather than assumed.

## Contributions

- A face-plus-voice Parkinson's screen in which no disease label touches any fit -- the reference is training controls only, normalisation constants are frozen at fit time, and a subject can be scored in isolation without reference to other test subjects.
- A synthetic-dysarthria contrastive activation direction in HuBERT space, built by degrading control speech with time-stretch and breathiness rather than by contrasting labelled patients against labelled controls.
- The alignment principle: a measurable precondition stating that a synthetic-degradation CAA detector works when the cosine between the synthetic and the real disease direction is positive, confirmed by +0.37 for voice with AUROC 0.765 and -0.48 for face with AUROC at chance.
- A mechanistic account of the modality asymmetry: HuBERT is trained on raw speech and so encodes the acoustic phenomenon that dysarthria is, while a FER2013-trained expression ViT places its disease signal in static appearance roughly orthogonal to facial motion, which is why a synthetic hypomimia degradation points the wrong way and a direction-free anomaly score recovers the signal instead.
- An integrity audit that reports its own failure: the encoder-selection transfer check recovers the voice choice but not the face choice, and the authors downgrade their headline accordingly.

## Method

Two frozen pretrained encoders and two scoring primitives, with all fitting done on training controls only and disease labels reserved for evaluation and for a post-hoc analysis. For voice, a contrastive activation addition direction is built in HuBERT space as the mean-activation contrast between control speech and the same speech synthetically degraded toward hypokinetic dysarthria by time-stretching and adding breathiness; a test clip is scored by projecting its centred embedding onto that direction. For face, no direction is used: a k-nearest-neighbour anomaly score measures mean distance to the training-control embedding cluster of a face-expression Vision Transformer. Normalisation constants are estimated on controls and frozen, so each score is a function of one input video and a subject can be scored in isolation. The two scores are combined by equal-weight late fusion. The paper's analytical contribution is the alignment principle: a derivation predicting that a synthetic-degradation CAA detector works when the cosine between the synthetic direction and the real disease direction is positive, and scores at or below chance otherwise -- a quantity that can be measured directly once labels are available for audit. Evaluation is on the YouTubePD benchmark, test subset n=157 with 20 PD and 137 controls, so prevalence is 13% and naive accuracy is uninformative at 0.87; reporting therefore uses AUROC, F1 and negative predictive value at the Youden-optimal operating point, with bootstrap confidence intervals.

## Results

The alignment principle is confirmed in both directions on the two modalities: the measured cosine between synthetic and real disease directions is +0.37 for HuBERT and -0.48 for the face-expression ViT, and correspondingly voice CAA reaches AUROC 0.765 while an anti-aligned face 'hypomimia' CAA direction scores about 0.50, chance. The face signal is recoverable by the direction-free anomaly primitive instead (AUROC 0.751), and equal-weight fusion reaches 0.802 with a 95% interval of [0.70, 0.89], sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.81, NPV 0.95 and PPV 0.35. Across three speech encoders AUROC tracks the cosine monotonically -- SEW-D at +0.24 gives 0.619, wav2vec 2.0 at +0.28 gives 0.728, HuBERT at +0.37 gives 0.765 -- though this is three points. The face-encoder ablation shows the choice matters enormously and is not explained by general representational quality: the FER2013-trained expression ViT reaches 0.751 while DINOv2 scores 0.41, CLIP 0.30, MARLIN 0.47 and a sibling expression encoder 0.47, all at or below chance. Against the published YouTubePD baselines, the label-free voice detector alone improves F1 from 0.27 to 0.43 over the supervised audio-only baseline and the fused system reaches 0.47, while the supervised face baseline at 0.86-0.92 AUROC remains well ahead -- which the authors state plainly rather than claiming state of the art. Four integrity audits are run and one of them fails informatively. Detector scores correlate near zero with face crop size, video length and frame rate; permuting test labels gives p < 0.01; within-test split-halves match the full-test AUROC inside the bootstrap interval. But the dev-to-test transfer audit, which asks whether the encoder choices could have been made without test labels, recovers the voice choice (HuBERT ranks first on dev and transfers) and does not recover the face choice: on the dev split the chosen face ViT ties DINOv2 at 0.629, and DINOv2 then scores 0.41 on test against the ViT's 0.751, so the +0.28 test margin is not identifiable from dev alone. The authors therefore report the face-side and fused AUROC as potentially optimistic and defer the face-encoder choice to pre-registered external validation. All results are on recorded video from one public benchmark; no clinical deployment or prospective data is involved.

## Limitations

Stated, and unusually forthrightly: the face encoder was selected in a way the dev split cannot justify, so the face and fused AUROC are labelled potentially optimistic pending external validation, and a definitive face-encoder choice is explicitly deferred. The system is framed as a rule-out triage screen and not a diagnostic -- NPV 0.95 is the operating use case while PPV is about 0.34 at 13% prevalence and would be lower in the community, so a positive output should trigger follow-up rather than a label. The dev split's PD voices are less separable than test's, verified with a model-free speaking-rate marker showing the PD-control gap widening from -0.37 SD on dev to -0.88 SD on test, and the authors decline to analyse the face modality's dev behaviour because it is inconsistent across encoders. Not stated but worth noticing: the test set contains 20 positive cases, so every clinical metric rests on a handful of subjects and the fused interval spans 0.70 to 0.89 -- wide enough that the fusion's 0.802 is not clearly separated from either single modality at 0.751 and 0.765. The alignment principle is validated on three voice encoders plus one face pilot, which is enough to show the sign is predictive but not enough to establish the monotone relationship between cosine and AUROC that the encoder table suggests. Everything is one benchmark of YouTube talking-head video, whose subjects, recording conditions and severity distribution are not a screening population, and the synthetic degradation is a hand-specified pair of transformations rather than anything validated against clinical dysarthria.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: Two things here transfer, and neither depends on the clinical domain. First, this is a use of a contrastive activation direction purely as a detector, with no steering at all, and it supplies the thing the archive has been missing for such directions: a falsifiable precondition, measurable in advance of the outcome, for whether a direction built from a proxy contrast points at the phenomenon of interest. The alignment principle says a synthetic-degradation CAA works when its cosine with the real direction is positive, and it is tested in both directions on the same paper -- +0.37 giving AUROC 0.765 for voice, -0.48 giving chance for face. Making a negative prediction and then confirming the failure is rare, and it is the shape of evidence the archive should want when a paper claims that a mean-difference direction encodes what its contrast pair was designed to encode. The mechanistic explanation is equally portable: the direction points the wrong way not because the concept is absent but because the encoder was trained for static emotion classification and places the relevant signal roughly orthogonal to motion, so what a contrast direction means depends on what the representation was trained to separate. That is the same lesson the archive holds about steering vectors whose contrast pairs vary along more axes than the intended one. Second, the encoder ablation is a caution about representational quality as a proxy for usability: DINOv2 and CLIP, far stronger general encoders, score at 0.41 and 0.30 under the identical anomaly protocol where a small FER2013-trained ViT reaches 0.751. A direction or a distance is a property of a specific representation, not of how good the model is. The dev-to-test audit is worth borrowing outright as a discipline -- ask whether your component choice could have been made without the labels you are reporting against, and if it could not, say so and mark the number optimistic, which is exactly what these authors do. The main caution in citing this: 20 positive cases, one benchmark, and the alignment principle validated on three encoders, so the sign result is convincing and the monotone cosine-to-AUROC relationship is not.

## Abstract

Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. Typical machine learning screening methods require PD labels, but the available data is limited by privacy concerns and the need for expert annotation. We propose a label-free face-plus-voice PD screen built entirely on frozen pretrained encoders--a face-expression Vision Transformer and HuBERT--in which no PD label touches any fit; the reference is training controls only. The voice modality uses a synthetic-dysarthria contrastive activation addition (CAA) direction built from time-stretch and breathy degradation of healthy speech; the face modality uses a k-nearest-neighbor anomaly score to the control embedding cluster. We introduce the alignment principle, a post-hoc analysis showing that a synthetic-degradation CAA detector works when the cosine similarity between the synthetic and real disease directions exceeds zero. Measured on the YouTubePD benchmark, this cosine is +0.37 for voice (CAA works, AUROC 0.765) and -0.48 for face (CAA fails; anomaly succeeds, AUROC 0.751). Equal-weight late fusion reaches AUROC 0.802 (95% CI [0.70,0.89]) with NPV 0.95, supporting a rule-out triage interpretation. An overfitting audit shows the voice detector transfers cleanly, while the face-side--and thus fused--AUROC is potentially optimistic pending external validation.
